bigcurve

The goal of bigcurve is to adaptively densify lines: insert vertices along great circle arcs exactly where a map projection bends them, and nowhere else. This is the adaptive resampling scheme of d3-geo by Mike Bostock, brought to R for paths and for segment meshes.

The error is controlled in the plane of the target projection: straight chords drawn between output vertices stay within tolerance (in projected units) of the true projected curve. By default the tolerance is derived from the projected extent: about one part in 2048 of the plot.

Installation

Once bigcurve is on CRAN:

install.packages("bigcurve")

The development version is on r-universe:

install.packages("bigcurve", repos = c("https://hypertidy.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org"))

Building from source needs the PROJ development library (libproj-dev on Debian/Ubuntu, proj-devel on Fedora, proj from Homebrew); Rtools on Windows has PROJ built in.

Example

We get just enough points to carry the curvature of a line from point A to point B (the shortest great circle distance) into a projection.

library(bigcurve)
crs <- "+proj=tmerc +lon_0=147 +lat_0=-42"
s <- segment(c(140, -164), c(-89, 80))
d <- densify(s, crs)
dim(d)
#> [1] 30  2

op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = rep(0.2, 4))
m <- do.call(cbind, maps::map(plot = FALSE)[1:2])
plot(d, type = "l"); lines(m); axis(1); axis(2)
text(s, lab = c("A", "B"), pos = 2)
plot(rproj_xy(d, crs), type = "l", asp = 1)

plot(rproj_xy(d, crs), type = "p", asp = 1)

points(rproj_xy(m, crs), pch = ".")
axis(1); axis(2)
par(op)

The same path in a different projection is the same path, densified differently, because the curvature is a different situation there.

crs2 <- "+proj=stere +lon_0=180 +lat_0=20"
d2 <- densify(s, crs2)
plot(rproj_xy(d2, crs2), type = "l", asp = 1)
points(rproj_xy(m, crs2), pch = ".")

Graticules and shared boundaries

densify() also works on segment meshes (rgl mesh3d style, vb vertices and is segment indices), and on vertex pool topology from wkpool, so any geometry that wk can read refines in one call. An edge shared by two neighbouring polygons gets the same new vertices from both sides.

## a coarse 30 degree world grid, as polygons
lon <- seq(-180, 150, by = 30)
lat <- seq(-60, 30, by = 30)
cells <- expand.grid(x = lon, y = lat)
wkt <- sprintf("POLYGON ((%s %s, %s %s, %s %s, %s %s, %s %s))",
               cells$x, cells$y, cells$x + 30, cells$y, cells$x + 30, cells$y + 30,
               cells$x, cells$y + 30, cells$x, cells$y)
pool <- wkpool::establish_topology(wk::wkt(wkt, crs = "OGC:CRS84"))

prj <- "+proj=laea +lon_0=0 +lat_0=-90"
out <- densify(pool, prj)
c(input = nrow(wkpool::pool_vertices(pool)),
  output = nrow(wkpool::pool_vertices(out)))
#>  input output 
#>    240    744

## back to geometry, then project with wk and PROJ (the fast general path)
geom <- wkpool::segments_to_wkb(out)
drawn <- wk::wk_transform(geom, PROJ::proj_trans_create(wk::wk_crs(geom), prj))
xy <- wk::wk_coords(drawn)
plot(range(xy$x), range(xy$y), type = "n", asp = 1, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
plot(drawn, add = TRUE)
points(xy$x, xy$y, pch = 19, cex = 0.3)

Output stays in longitude and latitude, so any projection tool can draw it; wk::wk_transform() with a PROJ::proj_trans_create() transform is the quickest general route for wk geometry, and rproj_xy() does the same for a plain coordinate matrix.

bigcurve and s2

s2 and bigcurve agree that an edge between two longitude, latitude points is a great circle arc. s2 works out what a shape is on the sphere (intersections, areas, distances); bigcurve draws that shape in any map projection with just enough vertices. The vignette walks through the difference: vignette("bigcurve-and-s2", package = "bigcurve").

Notes

Output coordinates are in the source coordinate system (geographic by default); project them for plotting, as above. Points that cannot be projected (beyond the horizon of an orthographic projection, say) never error: their segments are simply left alone, clipping is a job for another package.

The proper source of goodness is here:

https://bost.ocks.org/mike/example/
